answers.answer: In SCOPe 2.08 the three groups are placed as separate families within one superfamily: Ferritin (a.25.1.1, sunid 47241), Ribonucleotide reductase-like (a.25.1.2, sunid 47253) and Manganese catalase (T-catalase) (a.25.1.3, sunid 100951) all sit under the Ferritin-like superfamily a.25.1 (sunid 47240), within the Ferritin-like fold a.25 (sunid 47239) of the all-alpha class a. The correct reading is therefore: (1) Shared superfamily = SCOPe curators judged them probable homologs, descended from a common ancestor, despite low or undetectable sequence similarity. The curator comment on a.25.1 gives the key argument: the superfamily 'contains bimetal-ion centre in the middle of the bundle', i.e. a conserved, positionally equivalent dinuclear metal site built from the same helices of the four-helix bundle, a feature too specific to arise by convergence alone. (2) Separate families = the groups have diverged so far that they are not grouped at the family level, which is the strongest SCOPe evolutionary tier (clear sequence or close structure/function relatedness). Their different chemistries reflect this divergence: ferritins use a di-iron ferroxidase site to oxidise Fe(II) and store iron in a cage; RNR R2-like proteins use a di-iron (or Mn/Fe) site to generate a tyrosyl radical or activate O2 for hydroxylation, desaturation, etc.; Mn catalases use a dimanganese site to disproportionate H2O2. The same ancestral bimetal scaffold has been recruited to different metals and reactions. Note that the RNR-like family itself already spans very different enzymes (RNR R2, methane monooxygenase hydroxylase alpha/beta, stearoyl-ACP desaturase, toluene/o-xylene monooxygenase subunits, PaaC), showing that even family membership in SCOPe does not imply identical chemistry. (3) The fold level (a.25, 'core: 4 helices; bundle, closed, left-handed twist; 1 crossover connection') is weaker still: other a.25 superfamilies such as Cobalamin adenosyltransferase-like (a.25.2), EsxAB dimer-like (a.25.3) and PE/PPE dimer-like (a.25.4) share only the bundle topology and are not asserted to be homologous to ferritins; shared fold alone must not be read as homology. (4) Class a (all-alpha) carries no evolutionary meaning. Limits: superfamily membership supports a common origin and a shared metal-binding core, but it does not license transferring specific function, substrate, metal identity (Fe vs Mn), oligomeric state (24-mer cage vs dimer/hexamer) or catalytic mechanism between families; such transfer requires independent biochemical/spectroscopic evidence and active-site residue conservation checks. Using ferritin as a modelling template for an RNR R2 or Mn-catalase sequence is reasonable only for the helical core and metal-ligand positions, not for peripheral elements or ligand/oligomer interfaces. Also, a.25.1.3 is annotated as 'automatically mapped to Pfam 05067', and each family contains 'automated matches' protein entries (e.g. sunids 190435, 190575) assigned by sequence pipeline rather than manual curation, so family-level claims for those members carry less curatorial weight. Finally, SCOPe's superfamily grouping is a curated hypothesis; some ferritin-like superfamily members (e.g. YciF-like, half-ferritin, Rv2844-like families a.25.1.4-a.25.1.9) were added with structural rather than functional evidence, so the superfamily should be seen as a 'ferritin-like dinuclear metal bundle' clan, with chemistry varying by family.
evidence_used: pretrained knowledge of ferritin, RNR R2 and Mn catalase chemistry

answers.answer: In SCOPe 2.08 the three groups are placed as separate families within one superfamily: Ferritin (a.25.1.1, sunid 47241), Ribonucleotide reductase-like (a.25.1.2, sunid 47253) and Manganese catalase (T-catalase) (a.25.1.3, sunid 100951) all sit under the Ferritin-like superfamily a.25.1 (sunid 47240), within the Ferritin-like fold a.25 (sunid 47239) of the all-alpha class a. The correct reading is therefore: (1) Shared superfamily = SCOPe curators judged them probable homologs, descended from a common ancestor, despite low or undetectable sequence similarity. The curator comment on a.25.1 gives the key argument: the superfamily 'contains bimetal-ion centre in the middle of the bundle', i.e. a conserved, positionally equivalent dinuclear metal site built from the same helices of the four-helix bundle, a feature too specific to arise by convergence alone. (2) Separate families = the groups have diverged so far that they are not grouped at the family level, which is the strongest SCOPe evolutionary tier (clear sequence or close structure/function relatedness). Their different chemistries reflect this divergence: ferritins use a di-iron ferroxidase site to oxidise Fe(II) and store iron in a cage; RNR R2-like proteins use a di-iron (or Mn/Fe) site to generate a tyrosyl radical or activate O2 for hydroxylation, desaturation, etc.; Mn catalases use a dimanganese site to disproportionate H2O2. The same ancestral bimetal scaffold has been recruited to different metals and reactions. Note that the RNR-like family itself already spans very different enzymes (RNR R2, methane monooxygenase hydroxylase alpha/beta, stearoyl-ACP desaturase, toluene/o-xylene monooxygenase subunits, PaaC), showing that even family membership in SCOPe does not imply identical chemistry. (3) The fold level (a.25, 'core: 4 helices; bundle, closed, left-handed twist; 1 crossover connection') is weaker still: other a.25 superfamilies such as Cobalamin adenosyltransferase-like (a.25.2), EsxAB dimer-like (a.25.3) and PE/PPE dimer-like (a.25.4) share only the bundle topology and are not asserted to be homologous to ferritins; shared fold alone must not be read as homology. (4) Class a (all-alpha) carries no evolutionary meaning. Limits: superfamily membership supports a common origin and a shared metal-binding core, but it does not license transferring specific function, substrate, metal identity (Fe vs Mn), oligomeric state (24-mer cage vs dimer/hexamer) or catalytic mechanism between families; such transfer requires independent biochemical/spectroscopic evidence and active-site residue conservation checks. Using ferritin as a modelling template for an RNR R2 or Mn-catalase sequence is reasonable only for the helical core and metal-ligand positions, not for peripheral elements or ligand/oligomer interfaces. Also, a.25.1.3 is annotated as 'automatically mapped to Pfam 05067', and each family contains 'automated matches' protein entries (e.g. sunids 190435, 190575) assigned by sequence pipeline rather than manual curation, so family-level claims for those members carry less curatorial weight. Finally, SCOPe's superfamily grouping is a curated hypothesis; some ferritin-like superfamily members (e.g. YciF-like, half-ferritin, Rv2844-like families a.25.1.4-a.25.1.9) were added with structural rather than functional evidence, so the superfamily should be seen as a 'ferritin-like dinuclear metal bundle' clan, with chemistry varying by family.
